lesson.title: Space Complexity: What Your Algorithm Has to Remember
lesson.summary: Space complexity applies the same Big-O thinking to memory instead of time, measuring how much extra memory an algorithm needs as its input grows.
lesson.body:
Time complexity asks how many steps a piece of code takes. Space complexity asks a parallel question: how much extra memory does it need? Both use the same Big-O notation and the same instinct, ignore constants, focus on how the resource requirement grows as the input size n grows. An algorithm can be fast but memory hungry, or slow but memory frugal, and space complexity is how we describe that second half of the tradeoff.

Space complexity usually focuses on auxiliary space, the extra memory an algorithm allocates beyond the input itself. The input list you are given does not count against you; new lists, dictionaries, or other data structures your algorithm creates do. Consider two ways to reverse a list of n numbers.

def reversed_copy(values):
    result = []
    for v in reversed(values):
        result.append(v)
    return result

def reverse_in_place(values):
    left, right = 0, len(values) - 1
    while left < right:
        values[left], values[right] = values[right], values[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1

reversed_copy builds a brand new list that grows to hold all n elements, so its auxiliary space is O(n). reverse_in_place only ever uses two integer variables, left and right, no matter how large values is, so its auxiliary space is O(1), constant space, even though it still takes O(n) time to swap all the pairs.

This example shows why space complexity has to be tracked separately from time complexity: reverse_in_place and reversed_copy have the same time complexity, O(n), but very different space complexity, O(1) versus O(n). Neither number tells you the whole story alone. A programmer working on a device with limited memory might prefer reverse_in_place even if it is a few microseconds slower, while a programmer who needs to keep the original list unchanged has no choice but to accept the O(n) space of reversed_copy.

A doubling thought experiment works here too. If a function's auxiliary space is O(n) and it uses roughly 8 megabytes of extra memory for an input of 1 million items, you should expect it to need roughly 16 megabytes for 2 million items. If a function is O(1) in space, doubling the input should not noticeably change its memory footprint at all, since it is not creating new structures whose size depends on n.

One subtlety worth flagging: recursive functions carry hidden space cost in their call stack. A recursive function that calls itself n times before returning uses O(n) space for those stacked calls, even if it never explicitly creates a list or dictionary. This is easy to miss because the code has no visible container growing in size, but each pending function call still occupies memory until it returns.

As with time complexity, space complexity is expressed with the same set of growth rate classes, O(1), O(n), O(n^2), and so on, that the rest of this unit explores. Whenever you analyze an algorithm, it is good practice to ask both questions: how does its time grow, and how does its memory grow?
